results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across number sets (with >=18 responses) of each set's overall yes-rate; observed above the null means sets differ in how generously they are generalized more than the model predicts (model's set-level breadth is too compressed), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set differences.

results.name: upward_vs_downward_generalization
results.description: Over all sets, among targets 1-20 above the largest example vs 1-20 below the smallest example, yes-rate above minus below; observed above the null means people generalize upward (to larger numbers) more than downward, an asymmetry the model's symmetric size-distance similarity cannot produce (below means a downward bias).

results.name: recency_last_vs_first_example
results.description: In 2+-example sets, for non-example targets strictly closer in size to the last-shown example than the first (or vice versa), yes-rate for closer-to-last minus closer-to-first; observed above the null means people weight the most recent example more than the model's fitted recency (below means primacy / less recency than modelled).

results.name: drift_step_curvature
results.description: (yes-rate in trials 150-299 minus trials 0-149) minus (yes-rate in trials 300+ minus trials 150-299); positive observed above the null means the session drift toward "yes" is a front-loaded step/saturating jump rather than the steady linear relaxation the model assumes (below means the drift accelerates late).

results.name: even_gcd2_set_parity_contrast
results.description: In 2+-example sets that are all even with greatest common divisor exactly 2 (so the model's multiples-of-g rule, which needs g>=3, is silent), yes-rate for non-example even targets minus odd targets; observed above the null means people apply an explicit "even numbers" rule sharper than the model's parity-similarity dimension, below means the model over-weights parity.

results.name: square_set_square_target_contrast
results.description: In 2+-example sets whose examples are all perfect squares, yes-rate for non-example perfect-square targets minus non-square targets; observed above the null means people abstract a "square numbers" rule the model (no squareness feature) under-produces, below means the model over-produces it via factor similarity.
results.code:
# name: square_set_square_target_contrast
# description: In 2+-example sets whose examples are all perfect squares, yes-rate for non-example perfect-square targets minus non-square targets; observed above the null means people abstract a "square numbers" rule the model (no squareness feature) under-produces, below means the model over-produces it via factor similarity.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    sets = ns.unique()
    sq = set(i * i for i in range(1, 11))
    flag = {s: (len(s.split(",")) >= 2 and all(int(v) in sq for v in s.split(","))) for s in sets}
    exs = {s: set(int(v) for v in s.split(",")) for s in sets}
    fl = ns.map(flag).values.astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ident = np.fromiter((tt in exs[s] for tt, s in zip(t, ns.values)), bool, len(t))
    tsq = np.isin(t, list(sq))
    base = fl & ~ident
    a, b = base & tsq, base & ~tsq
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: low_evidence_item_drift
results.description: Among (set,target) cells that other responders mostly reject (leave-one-out cell yes-rate < 0.3), yes-rate on late trials (>=300) minus early trials (<150); observed above the null means the late "yes" drift reaches even clearly-bad items (lapse/guessing-like), which a logit criterion shift under-produces at the floor; below means the drift spares them more than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: low_evidence_item_drift
# description: Among (set,target) cells that other responders mostly reject (leave-one-out cell yes-rate < 0.3), yes-rate on late trials (>=300) minus early trials (<150); observed above the null means the late "yes" drift reaches even clearly-bad items (lapse/guessing-like), which a logit criterion shift under-produces at the floor; below means the drift spares them more than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    key = df["number_set"].astype(str) + "|" + df["target"].astype(str)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float)
    s = y.groupby(key).transform("sum").values
    n = y.groupby(key).transform("size").values.astype(float)
    yv = y.values
    ok = n > 1
    loo = np.where(ok, (s - yv) / np.maximum(n - 1, 1), np.nan)
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(float).values
    sel = ok & (loo < 0.3)
    l, e = sel & (ti >= 300), sel & (ti < 150)
    if l.sum() == 0 or e.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(yv[l].mean() - yv[e].mean())

results.name: high_evidence_item_drift
results.description: Among (set,target) cells that other responders mostly endorse (leave-one-out cell yes-rate > 0.7), yes-rate on late trials (>=300) minus early trials (<150); observed below the null means people become less consistent on clearly-good items late (drift is noise/lapses, not a pure criterion relaxation), above means the late "yes" shift is stronger at the ceiling than the model's logit shift allows.
results.code:
# name: high_evidence_item_drift
# description: Among (set,target) cells that other responders mostly endorse (leave-one-out cell yes-rate > 0.7), yes-rate on late trials (>=300) minus early trials (<150); observed below the null means people become less consistent on clearly-good items late (drift is noise/lapses, not a pure criterion relaxation), above means the late "yes" shift is stronger at the ceiling than the model's logit shift allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    key = df["number_set"].astype(str) + "|" + df["target"].astype(str)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float)
    s = y.groupby(key).transform("sum").values
    n = y.groupby(key).transform("size").values.astype(float)
    yv = y.values
    ok = n > 1
    loo = np.where(ok, (s - yv) / np.maximum(n - 1, 1), np.nan)
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(float).values
    sel = ok & (loo > 0.7)
    l, e = sel & (ti >= 300), sel & (ti < 150)
    if l.sum() == 0 or e.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(yv[l].mean() - yv[e].mean())
